paras: The killing of James Ross was the fatal shooting of a 40-year-old Black man by Biloxi police officer R. M. Randolph on the afternoon of July 31, 1910, in Biloxi, Mississippi. A coroner's jury found the killing justifiable homicide the same day, and the only known report, a special dispatch to The Hattiesburg News, presented it as the end of a drunken rampage.

According to the dispatch, Ross began the afternoon by running Henry Prados, described as 'another negro,' out of his own house. He then went out Division street, where he was said to have cursed Lawrence Hilderbrand, a white man, and insulted women walking past him. The paper added that 'it is thought' Ross was under the influence of liquor.

As Randolph approached, Ross was quoted as saying he did not care for 'Mun Randolph,' and the officer ordered him to drop a knife and consider himself under arrest. In the dispatch's account, Ross slashed at the officer, who backed away and fired twice over his head. When Ross lunged again, Randolph shot him through the right breast, and after a further lunge shot him through the head, killing him at about 4 o'clock.

A coroner's jury heard 'a number of witnesses' and returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, releasing the officer. The testimony is not reported, and no account from Prados, Hilderbrand or anyone on Ross's side appears in the coverage.

The Hattiesburg News carried the story on its front page on August 1 under the headline 'Officer Released by Coroner's Jury' and the deck 'Negro Ran Amuck And Insulted Women.' Its account followed the officer's version throughout, calling Ross 'a bad negro,' 'a terror among the members of his race here' and 'the desperado,' and describing Randolph as 'the plucky officer.' Explaining why the warning shots failed, it said that 'the negro had blood in his soul.'
No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found to have reported the killing in August or September 1910.

reader.title: Killing of James Ross
bases: A Biloxi police officer shot and killed James Ross while trying to arrest him; no crowd or mob took part (A1).
The only report found is one special dispatch to The Hattiesburg News (A1); no second white or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Biloxi special dispatch (officer's side)
accounts.gist: Ross, drunk according to what 'is thought', attacked several people, refused to drop a knife and slashed at Randolph; the officer fired two warning shots and then shot him twice, killing him. The coroner's jury found justifiable homicide.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Officer Released by Coroner's Jury' and 'Negro Ran Amuck And Insulted Women'; the text calls Ross 'a bad negro' and 'the desperado', says 'the negro had blood in his soul', and praises 'the plucky officer'.

record_check.dossier: Accused of attacking Henry Prados, cursing a white man, insulting women, resisting arrest and slashing at the officer with a knife (officer-side account)

record_check.record: resisted arrest; made several attempts to cut the officer with a knife
record_check.dossier: Supported as the paper's stated justification; it comes only from the officer's side, and the coroner's jury found justifiable homicide

info: About 4 p.m. on July 31, 1910 ('yesterday afternoon' in a dispatch dated Aug. 1)
Biloxi; Ross was on Division street before the shooting
James Ross, described as 'a negro, aged 40'
Accused of running Henry Prados, a Black man, out of his own house, cursing Lawrence Hilderbrand, a white man, insulting women passing by, resisting arrest and slashing at the officer with a knife
Officer released by the coroner's jury

sources.note: Special from Biloxi, Aug. 1: Officer R. M. Randolph shot and killed James Ross, 'a negro, aged 40'; coroner's jury found justifiable homicide; officer-side narrative only.
quotes: James Ross, a negro, aged 40, was shot and instantly killed by Police Officer R. M. Randolph, about 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon.
The coroner's jury, after hearing a number of witnesses in the case, rendered a verdict of justifiable homicide.
Ross, who was known to be a bad negro, and who was a terror among the members of his race here
who backed off and shot twice over the negro's head, trying thus to frighten him, but the negro had blood in his soul.
It is thought the negro was under the influence of liquor.
